strengths: Addresses an important and underexplored application area—primate behavior recognition—with potential impact for ethology, ecology, and conservation.

Introduces PriVi, a large-scale primate-centric video pretraining dataset (424 hours; 720k snippets) combining 174 hours of research/observational footage from 11 settings with 250 hours of curated YouTube video, plus bounding boxes and CLIP embeddings; the majority of the dataset is promised for release.

Provides a scalable data curation pipeline using CLIP-embedding relevance filtering, cut detection, and Grounding DINO zero-shot primate detection, with reported validation performance (e.g., 90.3% precision / 82.8% recall for relevance filtering; 82.7 mAP on PanAf500 detection).

Shows that domain-related V-JEPA pretraining on PriVi improves over human-centric VideoMix2M pretraining across four primate benchmarks, with both YT-Filtered and R&O components contributing to gains (Table 2).

Demonstrates that broad PriVi pretraining is more effective than in-domain pretraining on ChimpACT/PanAf500 alone, and that optional unlabeled in-domain continual pretraining further improves class-balanced metrics (Tables 2–3).

Reports strong empirical results: a lightweight frozen attentive classifier (220k parameters) surpasses or matches larger specialist and fully finetuned baselines across PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, and ChimpBehave (Table 4).

Ablations support several design choices, including primate-centric cropping, linear downprojection, multi-layer self-attention, and class tokens; a single-layer classifier remains competitive, indicating useful learned representations (Table 5).
The paper is generally clear about training details, evaluation metrics, datasets, and limitations, and it promises code/models for reproducibility.
weaknesses: The core methodological contribution is incremental: it applies existing V-JEPA/SSL pretraining and an attentive classifier to a new domain, while the curation pipeline largely relies on off-the-shelf components (CLIP, cut detector, Grounding DINO).
The dataset is not fully released: one source dataset comprising 14% of pretraining data is withheld, which limits exact reproducibility and full verification of the claimed dataset contribution.

Evaluation is narrow relative to the “general-purpose primate” framing: experiments cover only chimpanzees and baboons, and all reported evaluations use ground-truth bounding boxes, so real-world wild deployment without annotations is not tested.

The abstract claims the approach “scales favorably with fewer labels,” but the paper does not provide few-shot or label-efficiency experiments/learning curves; it trains downstream classifiers on full labeled datasets and reports frozen evaluation rather than varying label budgets.

Potential overlap/contamination between pretraining videos and downstream benchmark datasets is not analyzed or discussed; since YouTube and research videos may share source material with evaluation datasets, reported gains could be inflated.

Some comparisons may not be fully apples-to-apples: in-domain continual pretraining uses unlabeled target-domain videos that may not be available to all baselines, some prior methods are reimplemented under incompatible protocols (e.g., AlphaChimp), and several baselines are missing on some datasets.

The curation pipeline still involves manual choices—selecting 19 playlists and labeling 2,500 images by one annotator—raising scalability and potential bias concerns; inter-annotator agreement is not reported, and subsampling proportions are heuristic without ablation.

There are minor inconsistencies and omissions: YT-Random is described as “same size” as YT-Filtered, but Table 2 lists 280 h vs. 250 h; statistical significance/variance is not reported for small-dataset gains; and no broader-impact or ethics discussion is included despite scraped video and primate data.

strengths: Addresses a valuable and under-served problem—primate behavior recognition in the wild—with a data-centric framing that is well motivated for ecology, cognition, and conservation research, where expert manual annotation is a real bottleneck.

Introduces PriVi, a large-scale pretraining dataset (424 h: 174 h of research/observational footage plus 250 h of curated YouTube), which is substantially larger and more diverse than existing primate behavior datasets, and provides a sensible composition breakdown by genus/family and setting (Table 1).

The data curation pipeline is thoughtful and scalable: relevance filtering via CLIP embeddings with a lightweight MLP (82.8% recall, 90.3% precision, ROC-AUC 95.9%), cut detection, zero-shot primate detection with Grounding DINO (82.7 mAP on PanAf500), and source-dependent subsampling. The YT-Random vs. YT-Filtered ablation (Table 2) supports the claim that curation matters.

Frozen evaluation with a compact attentive classifier (~220k parameters) is a useful protocol; it is competitive with or better than much larger specialist models (e.g., ChimpVLM 167M, full fine-tuning of VideoMAEv2) and with V-JEPA's own single/three-layer attentive heads, highlighting representation quality and parameter efficiency.

Evaluation is reasonably broad across four benchmark datasets (PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, ChimpBehave) with both class-balanced and unbalanced metrics, and the ablations (Tables 2, 3, 5) systematically isolate the contributions of dataset composition, primate-centric cropping, classifier depth, and continual in-domain pretraining.
Code, models, and the majority of the dataset are promised to be released, which would be a meaningful resource for the community.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is limited. The core ingredients—V-JEPA self-supervised pretraining and a small self-attention classifier—are off-the-shelf; the paper's contribution is essentially applying an existing foundation model to a new domain plus a new dataset. This is a legitimate but relatively incremental technical contribution.

Some claims are somewhat overstated relative to the evidence. The abstract/Section 5.2 states the approach 'surpasses the state of the art on all four datasets across both class-balanced and unbalanced metrics,' yet the base PriVi row in Table 4 is below V-JEPA on BaboonLand balanced accuracy (33.99 vs. 34.57), and VideoMAEv2 has higher ChimpBehave B-Acc (74.8) than base PriVi (71.30). The all-metric superiority claim only holds for PriVi+CID, which relies on target-domain unlabeled data.

The 'general-purpose' framing is only partially validated: experiments are restricted to chimpanzees and baboons, even though the dataset is dominated by macaques (43%) with lemurs, marmosets, and orangutans also present. This species coverage gap is acknowledged in the limitations but undercuts the generality claim.
The dataset is not fully released (one source dataset comprising 14% of the pretraining data is withheld), which may limit exact reproducibility of the reported pretraining results.

The attentive classifier design (downprojection to D'=64, C learned class tokens) is somewhat ad hoc and not deeply motivated; the benefit of C class tokens is small (Table 5), and the downprojection choice is asserted rather than analyzed.

The curation pipeline is only compared against a random YouTube baseline (YT-Random); alternative curation/filtering strategies are not explored, so it is unclear how much the specific pipeline design (as opposed to simply more primate-centric data) drives the gains.

Evaluation relies on ground-truth bounding boxes for both training and evaluation cropping, which limits applicability to fully automatic in-the-wild deployment—an important caveat for the stated conservation use case.

strengths: Targets an under-served but scientifically important domain (primate behavior in the wild) and assembles a genuinely large-scale pretraining corpus (424 h spanning 11 research settings plus web video), which is a useful resource for the community.

The data curation pipeline is described concretely and supported by quantitative quality numbers (relevance classifier 82.8% recall / 90.3% precision; zero-shot detection 82.7 mAP on PanAf500), and the YT-Random vs. YT-Filtered comparison in Table 2 gives some evidence that curation matters.

The experimental suite is reasonably broad (four benchmarks: PanAf500, ChimpACT, BaboonLand, ChimpBehave) with ablations on dataset composition (Table 2), continual in-domain pretraining (Table 3), and classifier/backbone design (Table 5), and the frozen-evaluation protocol is sensible for low-label behavior datasets and cheap (11 h on 4 A100s).

Consistent evidence that domain-related pretraining beats human-centric pretraining (VideoMix2M) across the four datasets, and the primate-centric cropping ablation (Table 5) supports the design choice.
weaknesses: Methodological novelty is thin: the pipeline is essentially V-JEPA self-supervised pretraining on in-domain video plus a small attentive classifier head. The 'contribution' is largely the dataset and engineering, not a new learning approach; the architectural tweak (down-projection + C class tokens) is a minor modification with modest effect sizes.

The central SOTA claim is confounded. Table 4 states baselines are 'our own reproduction due to incompatible evaluation protocols' and that AlphaChimp 'solves a harder task by simultaneously predicting bounding boxes.' Comparing against self-reproduced numbers under differing protocols, and against methods trained with full fine-tuning while this work uses a frozen backbone, makes the headline 'outperforms prior work' claim apples-to-oranges.

The text overstates results in ways contradicted by its own tables. Section 5.2 claims PriVi+CID 'surpasses the state of the art on all four datasets across both class-balanced and unbalanced metrics,' yet in Table 4 PriVi+CID is worse than PriVi alone on PanAf500 Acc (85.01 vs 86.74). The naming is also inconsistent: text refers to 'PRIMA'/'PRIMA+CID' while tables say 'PriVi'/'PriVi+CID,' which undermines confidence in the reported comparisons.

Reported gains are modest and uneven (e.g., ChimpBehave Acc 94.62 -> 95.58; BaboonLand Acc 72.14 -> 75.43), and there is no analysis of when/why the method helps or fails, nor any comparison against simply fine-tuning the full backbone under the same protocol.
Reproducibility is limited: one source dataset comprising 14% of the pretraining data cannot be released, so the full pretraining corpus cannot be reconstructed or verified.

The 'general-purpose' framing is overstated relative to the evidence: evaluation covers only chimpanzees and baboons (the authors acknowledge this in Limitations), so generalization to other primates is asserted rather than demonstrated.

The relevance filter is a key component but its effect is only assessed via a YT-Random vs. YT-Filtered comparison; the downstream impact of its ~18% recall misses and ~10% false positives, and any error propagation into the pretraining set, is not characterized.
Some claims are unsupported by the presented evidence (e.g., 'scales favorably with fewer labels' in the abstract is not directly quantified, and no label-efficiency curve is shown).
